name: Greenhouse Automation System
description: Monitor temperature, humidity, and soil moisture in a model greenhouse and automatically control fan and pump when limits are exceeded.
guide:
What you will build

A miniature greenhouse that reads environmental sensors and automatically runs a fan when too hot and a water pump when soil is dry.

What you will learn

  • How multiple sensors work together in one control system
  • How setpoints and hysteresis prevent rapid on/off switching
  • How automated greenhouses support year-round food production

Safety first

  • Keep electronics dry and above water line
  • Use low-voltage pump and fan with teacher approval

You did it when…

  • LCD or Serial shows live temp, humidity, and soil readings
  • Fan turns on when temperature exceeds your max setpoint
  • Pump waters when soil moisture indicates dry conditions

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Build greenhouse frame
    Cardboard or clear plastic box ~40 cm — represents a small tunnel greenhouse.
  2. Install DHT11 and soil moisture sensor
    DHT on pin 2, soil analog on A0. Mount sensors inside the box.
  3. Connect fan and pump via relays
    Relay 1 pin 7 for fan, relay 2 pin 8 for pump. Never power motors from Arduino pins directly.
  4. Wire LCD (optional I2C)
    Display temp/humidity on line 1, soil status on line 2.
  5. Set thresholds in code
    Example: fan ON if temp > 32°C, pump ON if soil reading > 650 (dry).
  6. Test each actuator alone
    Blow hot air from hair dryer (teacher) to trigger fan. Dry soil to trigger pump.
  7. Log for one hour
    Record when fan/pump activated. Write how automation saves labour on farms.

Code to upload

Greenhouse controller (simplified) (Arduino C)

#include <DHT.h>
DHT dht(2, DHT11);
const int SOIL=A0, FAN_RELAY=7, PUMP_RELAY=8;

void setup(){
  dht.begin();
  pinMode(FAN_RELAY,OUTPUT); pinMode(PUMP_RELAY,OUTPUT);
}

void loop(){
  float t=dht.readTemperature();
  int soil=analogRead(SOIL);
  digitalWrite(FAN_RELAY, t>32 ? HIGH : LOW);
  digitalWrite(PUMP_RELAY, soil>650 ? HIGH : LOW);
  delay(2000);
}

name: Ultrasonic Distance Monitor
description: Measure distances with HC-SR04, display on Serial Monitor, and trigger LED alerts at set ranges.
guide:
What you will build

A distance meter that prints centimetres to your computer and lights green, yellow, or red LEDs based on how close an object is.

What you will learn

  • How sound pulses measure distance (time of flight)
  • How threshold zones create user alerts
  • Foundation for parking sensors and robotics

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Wire HC-SR04
    Trig 10, Echo 11, 5 V, GND.
  2. Add three LEDs
    Green pin 6, yellow 5, red 4 with resistors.
  3. Upload distance sketch
    Use pulseIn on Echo. distance = duration / 58 for cm.
  4. Open Serial Monitor 9600
    Move hand — values should update smoothly 2–400 cm.
  5. Set alert zones
    >50 cm green, 20–50 yellow, <20 red.
  6. Measure real objects
    Door width, desk height — compare with tape measure accuracy.

Code to upload

Distance zones (Arduino C)

const int TRIG=10,ECHO=11,G=6,Y=5,R=4;
long cm(){ digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW);delayMicroseconds(2);
 digitalWrite(TRIG,HIGH);delayMicroseconds(10);digitalWrite(TRIG,LOW);
 return pulseIn(ECHO,HIGH,30000)/58; }
void setup(){ pinMode(TRIG,OUTPUT);pinMode(ECHO,INPUT);
 pinMode(G,OUTPUT);pinMode(Y,OUTPUT);pinMode(R,OUTPUT);Serial.begin(9600);}
void loop(){ long d=cm(); Serial.println(d);
 digitalWrite(G,d>50); digitalWrite(Y,d>20&&d<=50); digitalWrite(R,d<=20&&d>0);
 delay(200);}

name: Servo Automatic Door Opener
description: Control a servo door latch with a potentiometer knob, then add a button for automatic open-and-close timing.
guide:
What you will build

A model door that opens when you turn a potentiometer or press a button, then closes automatically after a few seconds.

What you will learn

  • How servos move to precise angles
  • How analog knobs map to positions with map()
  • How timed automation works in access systems

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount servo on cardboard door
    0° = closed, 90° = open. Test range before gluing.
  2. Wire potentiometer
    Outer pins 5 V and GND, wiper to A0.
  3. Map knob to angle
    servo.write(map(analogRead(A0), 0, 1023, 0, 90));
  4. Add push button on pin 2
    On press: open to 90°, delay 3000 ms, return to 0°.
  5. Combine modes
    Use switch or second button to choose manual vs auto mode.
  6. Label door
    Draw diagram showing servo horn pushing latch bar.

Code to upload

Pot + button door (Arduino C)

#include <Servo.h>
Servo door;
const int POT=A0, BTN=2;
void setup(){ door.attach(9); pinMode(BTN,INPUT_PULLUP);}
void loop(){
  if(digitalRead(BTN)==LOW){ door.write(90); delay(3000); door.write(0); delay(500);}
  else door.write(map(analogRead(POT),0,1023,0,90));
}

name: Four-Way Traffic Intersection

What you will build

A tabletop intersection with four sets of red-yellow-green lights and pedestrian crossing buttons that extend green walk time.

What you will learn

  • How traffic phases sequence to prevent collisions
  • How state machines manage complex timing
  • Why pedestrian buttons request crossing time

Step-by-step instructions

  3. Wire pedestrian buttons
    Two buttons with pull-up on pins 22 and 23.
  4. Program phases
    Phase 1: Road A green. Phase 2: Road B green. Yellow between each change. All red before switch.
  5. Button extends walk
    If pressed during red for pedestrians, add 10 s to upcoming green walk phase (simplified demo).
  6. Test full cycle
    Time complete cycle. Ensure never two greens on crossing roads at once.

A biometric lock demo: scan enrolled finger → green LED and servo unlock; unknown finger → red LED and buzzer.

  5. Build door latch model

name: Sumo Wrestling Bot
description: Build a low, heavy push-bot that stays inside a ring and tries to push opponents out in a sumo tournament.
guide:
What you will build

A wide, low robot with a front bumper that drives forward searching for the opponent and pushes with maximum traction.

What you will learn

  • How centre of mass and wheel grip affect pushing power
  • How edge sensors (line sensors) detect ring boundary
  • Competition strategy and iterative design

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Design low chassis
    Keep centre of mass low — battery between wheels. Wide wheelbase resists tipping.
  2. Mount front bumper
    Flat plywood or acrylic across full width.
  3. Add edge IR sensors
    Five sensors under chassis pointing down — black ring border = edge detected.
  4. Search and charge code
    If no edge: full forward. If edge on left: turn right. If edge ahead: reverse and turn.
  5. Add opponent detection (optional)
    Ultrasonic: if object within 30 cm, boost motor power 100%.
  6. Practice on ring
    Draw 80 cm black circle on white board. Last robot inside wins.

Sumo edge avoid + charge (Arduino C)

name: Maze-Solving Robot
description: Build a robot that explores a wall maze using left-hand rule and remembers the path on a second run.
guide:
What you will build

A robot that navigates a simple grid maze with walls, using ultrasonic or IR side sensors and wall-following logic.

What you will learn

  • How maze algorithms (left-hand rule) guarantee exit in simply connected mazes
  • How sensors detect walls left, front, and right
  • How path memory improves second-run speed

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Build or print maze
    Grid on board with 15 cm cell size and 10 cm walls — start with 4×4 cells.
  2. Mount three ultrasonic or IR sensors
    Front, left, right facing walls.
  3. Implement left-hand rule
    Prefer turn left if open; else forward if open; else turn right; else U-turn.
  4. Log moves as string
    Store L/F/R in array during first run (e.g. FLFLL).
  5. Second run playback
    Replay move sequence without re-sensing (advanced) or re-run algorithm and compare time.
  6. Time both runs
    Document improvement and any wrong turns on first attempt.

What you will build

A robot that hugs the right wall at about 10 cm distance — useful for maze escape and corridor navigation.

  2. Target distance 10 cm

  3. Front sensor stop
    If front < 15 cm, turn left 90° in place.
  4. Test on L-shaped wall
    Robot should complete corner without hitting.
  5. Timed lap

name: Basic Car Robot (First Robot)
description: Assemble your first robot car, learn the parts, and measure how far it travels in a timed forward run.
guide:
What you will build

A simple two-wheel robot from a kit or cardboard that drives forward on command so you can calculate speed = distance ÷ time.

What you will learn

  • Names of chassis, motor, driver, and battery parts
  • How PWM controls motor speed
  • How to measure speed experimentally

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Identify all parts
    Label motors, wheels, driver board, Arduino, battery in notebook.
  2. Assemble chassis
    Follow kit instructions — wheels parallel, caster stable.
  3. Wire motor driver

  4. Upload forward sketch

  5. Measure distance
    Mark start line. Measure where robot stops. Repeat 3 times, average.
  6. Calculate speed
    speed = distance (m) ÷ time (s). Try PWM 100 vs 200 — which is faster?
  7. Draw labelled diagram
    Show power flow from battery → driver → motors.

name: Pick-and-Place Robot
description: Build a mobile robot with a servo gripper that picks up blocks and places them in a target zone.
guide:
What you will build

A robot that drives to a block, closes a gripper, reverses to a drop zone, and releases — mimicking factory pick-and-place.

What you will learn

  • How grippers use servos to open and close jaws
  • How sequenced moves replace continuous control
  • How industrial robots repeat precise cycles

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount gripper servo on front
    Open 120°, closed 40° — test on 3 cm cube.
  2. Mark pick and place zones
    Masking tape squares 50 cm apart on floor.
  3. Program state sequence
    Drive to pick → stop → close gripper → pause → reverse to place → open gripper.
  4. Use line or distance cues
    Stop at pick using front ultrasonic < 10 cm or crossing a line sensor.
  5. Refine timing
    Adjust drive seconds so robot stops centred in each zone.
  6. Run 5 cycles
    Count successful placements. Improve gripper foam padding if slips.

name: Python Chatbot
description: Create a rule-based chatbot in Python that answers questions about school subjects using if-else pattern matching.
guide:
What you will build

A terminal chatbot named “STEM Bot” that greets users, answers FAQs about maths/science, and says goodbye when user types quit.

What you will learn

  • How pattern matching on strings creates conversation
  • How loops keep programs interactive
  • Limits of rule-based bots vs learning systems

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Create chatbot.py
    Print welcome message.
  2. Main input loop
    while True: msg = input('You: ').lower()
  3. Add responses
    if 'hello' in msg: print('Hi! Ask me about STEM.')
  4. Subject answers
    elif 'photosynthesis' in msg: print short definition. Add 5 topics.
  5. Unknown handler
    else: print('I am not sure yet. Try another question.')
  6. Quit command
    if msg == 'quit': break
  7. Test with classmate
    List 10 questions that work and 3 that fail — plan improvements.

Code to upload

STEM Bot (Python)

print('STEM Bot ready. Type quit to exit.')
while True:
    msg = input('You: ').strip().lower()
    if msg == 'quit':
        print('Bot: Goodbye!'); break
    elif 'hello' in msg:
        print('Bot: Hello! Ask about science or maths.')
    elif 'photosynthesis' in msg:
        print('Bot: Plants use sunlight to make food from CO2 and water.')
    else:
        print('Bot: I will learn that soon.')

name: Scratch Platformer Game
description: Build a platform jumping game with a player sprite, platforms, enemies, and a lives system in Scratch.
guide:
What you will build

A side-view game: player jumps on platforms, avoids moving enemies, collects a star, and reaches the door to win.

What you will learn

  • How gravity and jumping change y velocity
  • How collision with colour or sprite detects ground
  • How lives and win conditions structure gameplay

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Choose player and platform sprites
    Draw or import character and several platform blocks.
  2. Gravity loop
    forever: change y by vy; vy -= 1 (gravity); if touching ground colour: set vy to 0.
  3. Jump on space
    if key space pressed and touching ground: set vy to 12.
  4. Left/right movement
    change x by 5 when arrow keys pressed.
  5. Enemy patrol
    Enemy moves x back and forth; if touching player: change lives by -1.
  6. Win door
    if touching door sprite: say You win! stop all.
  7. Start screen
    Green flag sets lives=3, score=0, player at start position.

name: Virtual Pet in Scratch
description: Create a virtual pet with hunger and happiness meters you manage by feeding, playing, and resting.
guide:
What you will build

A pet sprite whose hunger and happiness variables change over time — buttons feed, play, and sleep to keep it healthy.

What you will learn

  • How variables store game state
  • How timers simulate needs over time
  • How user actions restore meters

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Create variables hunger and happiness
    Both start at 80.
  2. Decay loop
    every 2 seconds: change hunger by -2, happiness by -1.
  3. Feed button
    hunger += 15 (max 100).
  4. Play button
    happiness += 15; hunger -= 5.
  5. Sleep button
    happiness += 5; stop decay for 5 seconds.
  6. Costumes by mood
    if happiness < 30: switch to sad costume; elif hunger < 20: tired costume.
  7. Game over
    if hunger <= 0: say Pet needs care! stop.

name: Weather App with API
description: Fetch live weather data from a public API and display temperature and conditions for your city in Python.
guide:
What you will build

A Python script that asks for a city name, calls a weather API, and prints current temperature and description (e.g. “Dar es Salaam: 28°C, partly cloudy”).

What you will learn

  • How APIs return JSON data over the internet
  • How to parse JSON with Python
  • How real apps use live external data

Safety first

  • Never commit API keys to public GitHub — use environment variables
  • Get API key from teacher; use free tier only

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Register for free API key
    OpenWeatherMap or similar with teacher help.
  2. Install requests
    pip install requests
  3. Build URL with city and key
    Read API docs for correct endpoint format.
  4. Parse JSON response
    temp = data['main']['temp']; desc = data['weather'][0]['description']
  5. Handle errors
    if city not found, print friendly message.
  6. Convert units
    Kelvin to Celsius if needed: temp - 273.15
  7. Extension
    Print 3-day forecast if API supports it.

Code to upload

Weather fetch (template) (Python)

import os, requests
city = input('City: ')
key = os.environ.get('WEATHER_API_KEY')
url = f'https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q={city}&appid={key}'
r = requests.get(url)
data = r.json()
if r.ok:
    t = data['main']['temp'] - 273.15
    print(city, round(t,1), 'C', data['weather'][0]['description'])
else:
    print('City not found')

name: Stomp Rocket Competition
description: Build foam rockets and a stomp launcher, then compete for maximum height and distance.
guide:
What you will build

A PVC stomp launcher and foam rocket with fins — launch by stomping an air bottle and measure apex height or range.

What you will learn

  • How compressed air creates thrust
  • How fin size affects stability vs drag
  • Fair testing with repeated launches

Safety first

  • Launch outdoors only, never at people
  • Wear eye protection when launching

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Assemble launcher
    PVC pipe, elbow, and 2-litre bottle — stomp bottle to push air through pipe.
  2. Build foam rocket body
    Foam tube fits loosely on pipe — not tight.
  3. Add fins
    Three equal fins at rear. Try small vs large fin sets on two rockets.
  4. Mark launch angle
    Hold launcher at 45° for distance or vertical for height trials.
  5. Measure
    Use clinometer or wall marks for height; tape for distance. Five launches each design.
  6. Winning design report
    Explain why lighter nose or bigger fins helped or hurt.

name: Parachute Drop Competition
description: Design parachutes from different materials and test which falls slowest from a fixed height.
guide:
What you will build

Three parachutes (plastic bag, fabric, tissue) carrying a small weight — you time descent from 4 m drop point.

What you will learn

  • How surface area increases air resistance
  • How terminal velocity depends on canopy size
  • How astronauts and drones use parachutes

Safety first

  • Drop only over clear area with teacher supervision
  • Do not climb unsafe heights — use approved balcony or ladder spot

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Cut three canopies
    Same diameter (40 cm) circle from different materials.
  2. Attach strings evenly
    8 strings tied around edge meeting at weight clip 30 cm below.
  3. Standardise weight
    Same metal washer or toy figure on all three.
  4. Drop protocol
    Release without throwing — let go from same height each trial.
  5. Time five drops each
    Average fall time. Slowest = most drag.
  6. Analyse
    Did holes or vents help stability? Optional: add small vent hole and retest.

name: Hot Air Balloon Model
description: Build a tissue paper hot air balloon and demonstrate lift using a hair dryer or tea light with teacher supervision.
guide:
What you will build

A lightweight tissue balloon envelope that rises when hot air inside is less dense than cool air outside.

What you will learn

  • How heated air expands and becomes buoyant
  • Why thin lightweight envelopes work best
  • Principles behind real hot air balloon flight

Safety first — critical

  • Open flame only with teacher — fire extinguisher nearby
  • Prefer electric hair dryer for classroom demos
  • Never fly near ceilings, trees, or power lines indoors

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Glue tissue panels
    6–8 gores into a teardrop envelope. Seal all seams airtight.
  2. Wire rim at opening
    Keeps mouth open for hot air entry.
  3. Attach lightweight basket
    Straws or thin card — minimal weight.
  4. Hair dryer test
    Hold dryer at opening until balloon feels taut, release gently.
  5. Measure max height indoors
    Mark ceiling touch height or time aloft.
  6. Explain buoyancy
    Write why hot air rises using density ideas from science class.

name: Balsa Wood Chuck Glider
description: Carve and balance a hand-launched balsa glider, then compete for longest flight distance.
guide:
What you will build

A lightweight balsa chuck glider thrown by hand — optimised for long straight glide after tuning wing and tail.

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Cut wing and fuselage from balsa
    Thin wing profile, sand leading edge round.
  2. Mount wing with slight dihedral
    Wing tips raised 2–3 cm for stability.
  3. Add tailplane and fin
    Adjustable with small shims.
  4. Balance at 1/3 chord
    Add clay nose weight until it balances on finger under wing.
  5. Test glide
    Gentle throw. If stalls, add nose weight; if dives, remove clay.
  6. Distance competition
    Three throws — best of three counts. Record design tweaks.

name: Flight Simulation Setup
description: Set up flight simulator software with a joystick, learn basic controls, and complete a takeoff-and-land checklist.
guide:
What you will build

A working flight sim station where each student completes a short lesson: taxi, takeoff, level flight, turn, and landing at a small airfield.

What you will learn

  • Names of flight controls: elevator, aileron, rudder, throttle
  • How pilots use checklists before flight
  • How simulation trains skills safely

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Install sim software
    Free option (e.g. GeoFS, FlightGear) or school-licensed sim with teacher.
  2. Connect USB joystick
    Calibrate axes in system settings — pitch, roll, yaw respond smoothly.
  3. Learn cockpit view
    Identify horizon, airspeed, altitude indicators.
  4. Practice takeoff
    Full throttle, rotate at recommended speed, climb straight.
  5. Practice turns
    30° bank turns left and right maintaining altitude.
  6. Practice landing approach
    Reduce throttle, descend gently, flare before touchdown.
  7. Logbook entry
    Each student records date, aircraft type, and manoeuvres completed.

name: Architectural Scale Model
description: Choose a building, draw a 1:50 scale plan, calculate real dimensions, and build a cardboard scale model.
guide:
What you will build

A scale model of your school block or a simple house at 1:50 — every 1 cm on model equals 50 cm in reality.

What you will learn

  • How scale ratios convert between drawing and real size
  • How architects communicate designs in plans and models
  • How to measure and transfer dimensions accurately

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Measure real building
    Length, width, height in metres (pace count or tape with permission).
  2. Convert to model cm
    real_cm = metres × 100; model_cm = real_cm ÷ 50.
  3. Draw floor plan on graph paper
    One square = 1 cm on model.
  4. Cut cardboard walls
    Score fold lines for corners. Label each piece with real dimension note.
  5. Assemble and glue
    Check right angles with set square.
  6. Add roof and label scale
    Place 1:50 scale bar on base board.
  7. Present
    Explain one calculation example to class (e.g. 10 m wall = 20 cm on model).

name: Sports Statistics Analysis
description: Collect sports match data, calculate averages and trends, and create charts to support a short prediction.
guide:
What you will build

A statistics report on a local football team or class tournament: goals per match, mean, median, bar chart, and one evidence-based prediction.

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Choose dataset
    At least 8 matches or class games with scores recorded.
  2. Build table
    Columns: match, goals for, goals against.
  3. Calculate mean goals
    Sum ÷ number of matches. Find median too.
  4. Draw bar chart
    Goals per match on paper or spreadsheet.
  5. Trend question
    Are goals increasing over season? Compare first half vs second half average.
  6. Prediction
    Predict next match score range using mean ± 1 goal. State confidence in one sentence.

name: Data Collection and Graphing
description: Survey your class on a topic, organise results in a table, and present bar and pie charts with interpretation.
guide:
What you will build

A class survey project (favourite subject, transport to school, etc.) with tally table, bar chart, pie chart, and written interpretation.

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Write one survey question
    4–5 answer options maximum.
  2. Collect 30 responses
    Tally marks in notebook — one person one vote.
  3. Frequency table
    Category and count columns; add total row.
  4. Bar chart
    Label axes, equal bar widths, title.
  5. Pie chart
    Convert counts to degrees: angle = (count/total)×360°.
  6. Interpret
    Two sentences: most popular answer and what surprised you.

name: Geometric Tessellation Art
description: Create repeating tile patterns that fill a plane without gaps, inspired by Islamic geometric art or Escher designs.
guide:
What you will build

A colour tessellation poster using one repeating shape (triangle, square, or hexagon modifications) that tiles across an A3 sheet with no overlaps or gaps.

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Study examples
    Look at honeycomb (hexagons) and square floor tiles — note no gaps.
  2. Choose base shape
    Start with equilateral triangle or square on card.
  3. Modify one side
    Cut a bump on one edge and matching bite on opposite — shape still tiles.
  4. Trace repeating pattern
    Trace tile repeatedly on large paper; align carefully.
  5. Colour alternating tiles
    Two or three colours so neighbours differ.
  6. Write maths note
    State which transformations (translation, rotation) you used.

name: Population Growth Modeling
description: Model population growth with exponential and logistic equations using spreadsheet or Python and real country data.
guide:
What you will build

A table and graph of population over 20 years using real starting data, comparing simple exponential growth with a logistic (leveling-off) model.

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Get starting population
    Use published data for Tanzania or your region (teacher-provided).
  2. Exponential model
    P(next) = P × (1 + r) with r = 2.5% = 0.025 per year in spreadsheet.
  3. Plot 20 years
    Year vs population on graph paper or Excel.
  4. Logistic extension
    Cap at carrying capacity K — growth slows as P approaches K.
  5. Compare models
    Which matches recent real data better? Why exponential fails long-term.
  6. Write prediction paragraph
    What happens to schools and jobs if population keeps growing?

Code to upload

Exponential growth in Python (Python)

P = 1_000_000
r = 0.025
for year in range(21):
    print(year, int(P))
    P = P * (1 + r)

name: Solar Panel Angle Optimization
description: Measure how solar panel angle affects voltage output and find the best tilt for your location at noon.
guide:
What you will build

An experiment tilting a small solar panel at 0°, 15°, 30°, 45°, and 60° while measuring output voltage at solar noon.

What you will learn

  • How sun angle affects energy collected
  • How to find maximum using systematic tests
  • Why countries use different optimal tilts by latitude

Step-by-step instructions

  1. Mount panel on adjustable protractor rig
    Secure multimeter leads to panel output.
  2. Test on sunny day at noon
    Record voltage at each angle. Three readings averaged.
  3. Graph angle vs voltage
    Identify peak angle.
  4. Compare to latitude rule
    Rule of thumb: tilt ≈ latitude for year-round. Tanzania ~6°S → discuss ~6–10° tilt.
  5. Recommend installation
    Write one paragraph for school roof panel placement.
